In [Class 26](26_Class.qmd), the boundary of an elastic body was divided once for each direction, and in [Class 28](28_Class.qmd), the prescribed displacements and tractions entered the matrix equations through the ID array and the element force vector.
The way each kind of boundary condition is imposed is the same as for the Poisson Equation, applied to one component of the displacement at a time.
However, for elasticity, boundary conditions not only represent different behavior, but they also have different requirements.
Every support drawn on a model is an idealization of a real connection, such as a bolt, a bearing, a weld, or the soil under a footing, and the choice of idealization often affects results.
This class works to clarify some of those decisions.

## Three kinds of boundary conditions for elastiticy

| Kind | Poisson Equation | Elasticity, for each direction $i$ | How it enters the matrix equations |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Dirichlet | $u = g$ on $\Gamma_g$ | $u_i = g_i$ on $\Gamma_{g_i}$ | $\mathrm{ID}(i, A) = -1$, and the known values move to the right-hand side through $-\sum_b \underline{\underline{k}}^e_{ab}\,\underline{g}_b$ |
| Neumann | the flux is $h$ on $\Gamma_h$ | the traction is $\sigma_{ij}n_j = h_i$ on $\Gamma_{h_i}$ | $\int N_a\,h_i\,d\Gamma$ over the element sides on $\Gamma_{h_i}$ |
| Robin | $\hat{a}\,u$ plus the flux is $\hat{c}$ on $\Gamma_r$ | a spring support, $\sigma_{ij}n_j + k_s\,u_i = \hat{c}_i$ | $\int N_a\,k_s\,N_b\,d\Gamma$ is added to $\underline{\underline{k}}^e$, and $\int N_a\,\hat{c}_i\,d\Gamma$ to $\underline{f}^e$ |

: The three kinds of boundary condition in the Poisson Equation and in elasticity. {#tbl-c29-kinds}

A free surface is a Neumann boundary on which both components of the traction are zero, so it requires no computation at all.
A pressure $p$ pushing on a surface is a traction along its normal, $\underline{h} = -p\,\underline{n}$, so on a surface that is not aligned with the axes, both components of the traction are nonzero.

The Robin condition describes an **elastic support**, in which the surface is held by springs whose stiffness per unit area is $k_s$, so that the traction is $h_i = -k_s\,u_i$.
Examples are the soil under a slab or footing, a rubber bearing pad under a bridge girder, and the flexibility of a bolted connection.
As in [Class 22](22_Class.qmd), a very stiff spring behaves like a fixed support, and a very soft one like a free surface.
Soil can push on a slab but cannot pull on it, so a slab that lifts off the ground is described more accurately by springs that act only in compression.
That makes the problem nonlinear, which is beyond the scope of this course.

## Supports must prevent rigid-body motion

### Rigid-body motions

In [Class 23](23_Class.qmd), a temperature that is the same constant everywhere has no gradient, so it stores no energy, and the stiffness matrix of a body with only Neumann boundaries is singular.
In elasticity, the displacements that store no energy are those that produce no strain.
In two dimensions there are three of them, two translations and a rotation, which together are called the **rigid-body motions**:

$$
\underline{u}_r(\underline{x}) = \begin{bmatrix} c_0 - \theta\,x_1 \\ c_1 + \theta\,x_0 \end{bmatrix} ,
$$

where $c_0$ and $c_1$ are translations along $x_0$ and $x_1$, and $\theta$ is a small rotation about the origin.
Its strains are $\varepsilon_{00} = u_{0,0} = 0$, $\varepsilon_{11} = u_{1,1} = 0$, and $2\varepsilon_{01} = u_{0,1} + u_{1,0} = -\theta + \theta = 0$.
A body in three dimensions has six rigid-body motions, three translations and three rotations.

Since the basis functions reproduce linear fields exactly, every rigid-body motion can be represented by a vector of nodal displacements $\underline{d}_r$.
It produces no strain, so $a(\underline{w}^h, \underline{u}_r) = 0$ for every $\underline{w}^h$, and the stiffness matrix assembled before any supports are applied satisfies $\underline{\underline{K}}\,\underline{d}_r = \underline{0}$ for each of the three motions.
The supports must remove all three.
For a connected mesh, the stiffness matrix that remains after the prescribed rows and columns are removed is positive definite exactly when no rigid-body motion satisfies every support.
The mathematical result behind this is **Korn's inequality**, which bounds the size of a displacement by the size of its strain once the rigid-body motions are excluded, in the same way that a Dirichlet boundary bounds the temperature by its gradient in the Poisson Equation.

### Recognizing a mechanism

Each support component prevents one point from moving in one direction.
The direction in which it can push or pull on the body is called its **line of action**.
A rigid-body motion is described by three numbers, $c_0$, $c_1$, and $\theta$, so at least three support components are needed to prevent all of them.
Three are not always enough.
In two dimensions, the supports prevent every rigid-body motion unless the lines of action are all parallel, which leaves a translation free, or all pass through a single point, which leaves a rotation about that point free (@fig-c29-mech).
These are the same conditions that are used in statics to decide whether a body is held in place.
A body that can still move in this way is called a **mechanism**.

The arrangement in @fig-c29-mech c is easy to miss.
The pin prevents both translations, and the roller appears to prevent rotation, but a small rotation about the pin moves the point at the roller at right angles to the roller's line of action, and the roller allows that.

![Four ways of supporting a body, with the lines of action of the rollers dashed. (a) A pin and a roller: the three lines of action are neither parallel nor concurrent, and the body is held. (b) Three rollers with parallel lines of action: the body can slide along them. (c) A pin, and a roller whose line of action passes through the pin: the body can turn about the pin. (d) A ring on three rollers whose lines of action meet at its center: the ring can spin. In (b) to (d), the orange outline and arrow show the motion that is left free.](`{python} fig_mech_path`){#fig-c29-mech width=100%}

### Loads on a body that is not supported

In Class 23, a solution with only Neumann boundaries exists only if the total heat entering the body is zero, $\underline{1}^T\underline{F} = 0$.
In elasticity, multiplying $\underline{\underline{K}}\,\underline{d} = \underline{F}$ by $\underline{d}_r^T$ for each rigid-body motion gives $\underline{d}_r^T\underline{F} = 0$, so the loads must do no work on any rigid-body motion.
For the two translations and the rotation, this condition is

$$
\sum F_0 = 0, \qquad \sum F_1 = 0, \qquad \sum M = 0 ,
$$

which states that the applied loads are in equilibrium.
If they are, there are infinitely many solutions, which differ by a rigid-body motion, and if they are not, there is no static solution, because the loads would set the body in motion.
A spacecraft, a pressure vessel, and a test specimen pulled at both ends are loaded in this way.
Nothing holds them in place, but a finite element model of each still needs supports that remove the rigid-body motions, without resisting the deformation that the loads cause.
The next section describes such supports.

## Statically determinate and redundant supports

Supports with exactly three components whose lines of action are neither parallel nor concurrent are **statically determinate**.
The three equations of equilibrium of the whole body then determine the three reactions, whatever the material and the mesh.
Such supports only prevent rigid-body motion.
They cannot cause stress of their own, because the body is free to take whatever shape the loads produce.

Supports with more components are **statically indeterminate**, or **redundant**.
There are more reactions than equations of equilibrium, so the reactions depend on the stiffness of the body, and the supports can resist deformation that the loads would otherwise cause.
@fig-c29-red shows the difference for a steel plate, 200 mm by 100 mm and 10 mm thick, pulled at its right end by a uniform traction of 50 MPa.

- In (a), the left end rests on rollers that hold $u_0$, and its midpoint is also held in $u_1$.
  Under the pull, the plate stretches along $x_0$ and contracts along $x_1$ by the Poisson effect.
  The rollers allow the contraction, so the solution is the uniform stress $\sigma_{00} = 50$ MPa, with $\sigma_{11} = \sigma_{01} = 0$, which the elements reproduce exactly.
- In (b), the left end is clamped.
  The clamp prevents the contraction at the left end, and so it causes a stress $\sigma_{11}$ across the plate that the pull alone does not.
  This stress is largest at the clamp and has nearly disappeared about one depth of the plate away from it.
- The exact solution of the clamped plate has infinite stress at the two corners of the clamp, where a free edge meets a fixed one.
  As (c) shows, the largest stress in the finite element solution rises from `{python} f"{clamp_peaks[0]:.1f}"` MPa to `{python} f"{clamp_peaks[1]:.1f}"` MPa as the mesh is refined, and it continues to rise with further refinement.
  No mesh gives a converged value there.

The rollers in (a) also have more than three components, but they agree with the deformation that the pull causes, so they do not resist it.
Whether a support causes stress depends on whether it resists the deformation of the body, and supports that are statically determinate never do.

![A plate pulled at its right end by 50 MPa, with two idealizations of its left end. The color shows $\sigma_{11}$, the stress across the plate. (a) The left end on rollers, with its midpoint held in $u_1$: $\sigma_{11}$ is zero everywhere, to roundoff. (b) The left end clamped: the clamp prevents the Poisson contraction, which causes $\sigma_{11}$ near the clamp. (c) The largest $\sigma_{00}$ at any Gauss point as the mesh is refined, with twice as many elements along the plate as through its depth. With the rollers, it is exactly 50 MPa on every mesh; with the clamp, it grows without limit, because the exact stress at the corners of the clamp is infinite.](`{python} fig_red_path`){#fig-c29-red width=100%}

A uniform rise in temperature $\Delta T$ makes a body that is free to move expand by the strain $\alpha\,\Delta T$ in every direction, where $\alpha$ is the coefficient of thermal expansion, without any stress.
Statically determinate supports allow this expansion, so they cause no stress, while redundant supports that prevent it cause stresses that can be large.
Class 31 studies thermal stress in more detail.

### Reactions as a check

The rows of $\underline{\underline{K}}$ for the prescribed components were left out of the matrix equation in Class 28, but they are not discarded.
Let $\underline{\underline{K}}_{\text{complete}}$ be the stiffness matrix assembled for every displacement component, $2n_{np} \times 2n_{np}$ in two dimensions, before any rows or columns are removed.
Let $\underline{d}_{\text{complete}}$ hold every displacement component, the solved values from $\underline{d}$ at the unknown components and the prescribed values $g_{iA}$ at the others.
Let $\underline{F}_{\text{complete}}$ hold the applied loads, the body force and the tractions, for every component, without the terms that moved the prescribed displacements to the right-hand side.
The **reactions**, the forces that the supports apply to the body, are then

$$
\underline{R} = \underline{\underline{K}}_{\text{complete}}\,\underline{d}_{\text{complete}} - \underline{F}_{\text{complete}} .
$$

In the rows of the unknown components, this is zero, since those rows are the equations that were solved, so $\underline{R}$ is nonzero only at the prescribed components.
For a body without spring supports, $\underline{d}_r^T\underline{\underline{K}}_{\text{complete}} = \underline{0}^T$ for every rigid-body motion, so the reactions and the applied loads together always satisfy the three equations of equilibrium, whatever the mesh.
The sum of the reactions is therefore not a check on accuracy, but it is a useful check that the loads were applied where, and with the magnitude, that was intended.

When the supports are statically determinate, the reactions can be computed by hand from statics before the analysis, and the finite element reactions must agree with them.
When a body whose loads are already in equilibrium, such as a specimen pulled at both ends, is held by determinate supports only to remove its rigid-body motions, the reactions must be zero.
Nonzero reactions then show that the loads are not balanced as intended.

## Supports, interactively

The widget below models the plate of @fig-c29-red in plane stress, with 16 by 8 elements.
Any node on the boundary can be given a support, and the widget reports whether the supports leave a mechanism, whether they are statically determinate, and what the reactions are.

- Click a node on the boundary to change its support.
  Each click moves through a roller that holds the component normal to that side, a roller that holds the other component, a pin, and no support.
- Use the support buttons for common arrangements, and the load buttons to change the load.
- The dashed outline is the undeformed plate, and its dots are the nodes that can be clicked.
- When the supports leave a mechanism, the widget shows the motion that is free; otherwise it shows the deformed plate, magnified, colored by the von Mises stress.
  The supports, the applied loads (blue), and the reactions (green) are drawn where the nodes of the deformed plate have moved, so a pin stays in place and a roller moves along the surface it rolls on.
- The loads on the edges are uniform tractions, 5 MPa down on the top edge and 50 MPa along $x_0$ on the ends, and the temperature rise is uniform.
